newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen extending gains at open.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen extending gains at open.

text.p: Wall Street shares are expected to open higher on Wednesday, still basking after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan delivered an upbeat report on the U.S. economy to Congress yesterday.

The stock market, which surged on Tuesday when the Fed chief's comments put fears of an imminent interest rate hike to rest, should extend gains and draw further fuel from solid corporate earnings reports, analysts said.

"Greenspan gave a green light to markets yesterday," Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said. "The market will probably move higher this morning and continue to rally for the next day or two."
On Tuesday, the Dow Jones Industrial average soared around 155 points to close at a record 8061.65, after Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to a House Banking subcommittee.

Greenspan said the Fed would raise rates if needed to head off inflation but suggested that might not happen any time soon. He also avoided cautioning stock market investors about "irrational exuberance," as he had in the past.

Greenspan will address the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, in the second leg of the Fed's mandatory, semiannual testimony. He will repeat his formal remarks and then answer questions from Senators.
"This should be a restatement, a replay of yesterday," Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said. "It will probably be a non-event."
Fed Vice Chairwoman Alice Rivlin, Fed Governor Laurence Meyer and New York Fed President William McDonough will testify to the House Banking Committee starting at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.
In early trade, the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index rose 2.35 points at 944.60. The long bond was flat at a 6.42 percent yield.
Solid quarterly results should also boost share prices on Wednesday, analysts said.
Dow component Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Co (3M) posted second quarter earnings of $1.01 per share compared with $0.91 per share in last year's comparable quarter, on sales of $3.82 billion.
Several technology stocks also reported above-forecast results late Tuesday, analysts said.
The dollar, whose recent strength has given an added lift to financial markets, was sturdy again on Wednesday. It rose against the yen in Tokyo, trading at 115.32/42 yen.
In Europe, the dollar hovered below 1.83 marks, after setting 71-month highs.
Japan's Nikkei average closed down 26.51 points, or 0.13 percent, at 20,130.51.
In London, the FTSE 100 was up 66.7 at 4913.4.
U.S. stocks were slightly firmer in London trading.

The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that J.P. Bryan, chief executive of Gulf Canada Resources Ltd, has not made friends with his critical comments on Calagary's oil sector and his takeover style.

The New York Times said in its Market Place column that Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce has taken a big step towards forming a worldwide securities business, with its agreement to acquire Oppenheimer Holdings Inc.
